articles.title: The Five-Minute Night Review
articles.titleHinglish: Paanch Minute Ka Raat Wala Review
articles.content:
Most days are lived and then immediately deleted. You could not describe last Tuesday if someone asked. This is not a memory problem; it is that nothing was ever written down, and an unreviewed day leaves almost no trace.

The night review is the smallest useful practice in this entire app, and it takes about five minutes.

Four questions, written by hand or typed, kept short.

What went well today? One line. Not the achievements — the small thing. A conversation that went better than expected, a task you had been avoiding and finally started.

What took my peace? Also one line, and be specific. Not work was stressful, but: I checked my phone during the meeting and then spent an hour worrying about a message. Specific answers repeat, and repeated answers become the material you can actually work with.

What did I do to someone else? This is the question most people skip and the one that changes behaviour fastest. Were you short with someone who did not deserve it? Did you notice someone having a hard time and say nothing?

And what do I want to carry into tomorrow? One sentence. A thought, an intention, a specific repair to make.

That is the whole thing.

A few notes on doing it properly.

Keep it honest and unedited. A journal written for an imagined reader is useless. Nobody is going to read it, which is precisely what gives it value.

Do not turn it into an essay. Long entries get skipped on the days you most need them. Four lines survives a bad week; two pages does not.

Do it before the phone. The review works best as the last thinking of the day, not squeezed between videos.

And read back once a week. This is where the actual return is. Individual days say little; seven days together say a great deal — the same person appears in your peace-taking column three times, the same avoidance shows up on four days. Nothing is easier to fix than a pattern you can see written down in your own handwriting.

One honest note. Some nights the review will be bleak, and it is tempting to skip those. Those are the entries worth having. A record only of good days is not a record of your life; it is a highlight reel, and you already have enough of those on your phone.
articles.contentHinglish:
Zyadatar din jiye jaate hain aur turant delete ho jaate hain. Koi poochhe to aap pichhla Mangalvaar bata bhi nahi paoge. Yeh memory ki problem nahi hai; baat yeh hai ki kuch likha hi nahi gaya, aur bina review wala din lagbhag koi nishaan nahi chhodta.

Raat wala review is poore app ki sabse chhoti kaam ki practice hai, aur ismein lagbhag paanch minute lagte hain.

Chaar sawaal, haath se likhe ya type kiye, chhote rakhe hue.

Aaj kya achha gaya? Ek line. Badi kaamyabi nahi — chhoti cheez. Koi baat jo ummeed se behtar gayi, koi kaam jise aap taal rahe the aur aakhirkaar shuru kiya.

Mera chain kisne liya? Yeh bhi ek line, aur specific bolo. "Kaam mein stress tha" nahi, balki: meeting ke beech maine phone dekha aur phir ek ghanta ek message ki chinta mein nikala. Specific jawab dohraate hain, aur dohraaye gaye jawab wo maal hain jispar aap sach mein kaam kar sakte ho.

Maine kisi doosre ke saath kya kiya? Yeh sawaal zyadatar log skip karte hain aur yahi behaviour sabse tez badalta hai. Kya aap kisi ke saath rukhe the jo iske laayak nahi tha? Kya aapne dekha ki kisi ka waqt mushkil hai aur kuch nahi bola?

Aur kal main kya lekar chalna chahta hoon? Ek sentence. Ek soch, ek iraada, ya ek khaas marammat.

Bas, itna hi.

Theek se karne ke liye kuch baatein.

Imaandaar aur bina sudhaare likho. Jo journal kisi kaalpanik padhne wale ke liye likha jaata hai wo bekaar hai. Ise koi nahi padhega — aur wahi ise keemti banata hai.

Ise nibandh mat banao. Lambi entries theek un dinon skip hoti hain jab unki sabse zyada zaroorat hoti hai. Chaar line ek kharab hafta jhel leti hain; do page nahi.

Phone se pehle karo. Yeh review tab sabse achha chalta hai jab wo din ki aakhri soch ho, do videos ke beech thusi hui nahi.

Aur hafte mein ek baar peeche padho. Asli faayda yahin hai. Alag alag din kam bolte hain; saat din milkar bahut kuch kehte hain — wahi insaan aapke "chain lene" wale column mein teen baar aata hai, wahi taal-matol chaar dinon mein dikhti hai. Jo pattern aapki apni likhawat mein saamne likha ho, usse aasaan kuch bhi theek karna nahi hai.

Ek imaandaar baat. Kuch raatein review udaas hogi, aur unhe skip karne ka mann karega. Wahi entries rakhne laayak hain. Sirf achhe dinon ka record aapki zindagi ka record nahi hai; wo ek highlight reel hai, aur wo aapke phone mein pehle se kaafi hain.

articles.title: The First Twenty Minutes Decide More Than You Think
articles.titleHinglish: Pehle Bees Minute Aapki Soch Se Zyada Tay Karte Hain
articles.content:
There are two ways to begin a day. In the first, the phone is picked up before your feet touch the floor, and within ninety seconds you have absorbed a news headline, three work messages and someone's holiday. The day has started, and it started as a reaction to other people.

In the second, twenty minutes belong to you before anything else is allowed in.

This is not about being virtuous in the morning. It is about who sets the tone. Whatever enters first has an unfair influence on everything that follows, partly because the mind is unusually impressionable in that window and partly because a mood established early is what every later event gets interpreted through.

A workable twenty minutes looks like this, and none of it is dramatic.

Water and light first. Open a window or step outside. Both of these are simple physical signals that the day has begun, and they do more for alertness than the first coffee does.

Then ten minutes of stillness, in whatever form you keep. Sitting quietly, one thought held on purpose, or a short meditation. If ten is too much, do three. Three minutes done daily beats twenty minutes done rarely.

Then one line about the day. Not a task list — an intention. Today I want to be patient with my mother. Today I will finish the thing I have been avoiding. One sentence, and you will be surprised how often you remember it at exactly the moment it matters.

And only then, the phone.

A few practical protections. Charge the phone outside the bedroom, because willpower at 6am is not a real resource. Keep whatever you need — journal, mat, chair — set out the night before, so the morning has no decisions in it. And if you live in a full house, take the earliest slot available, even if it is only ten minutes before the others wake.

One honest allowance. Some mornings will be broken — a sick child, an early meeting, a night with no sleep. On those days, take the shortest possible version: one minute at the window, one deliberate breath, one sentence in your head. It sounds too small to matter. It is not, because what you are protecting is not the twenty minutes. It is the habit of beginning the day as yourself rather than as a respondent to everyone else.
articles.contentHinglish:
Din shuru karne ke do tareeke hain. Pehle mein, pair zameen par lagne se pehle phone haath mein aa jaata hai, aur nabbe second ke andar aap ek news headline, teen office ke message aur kisi ki chhutti soak chuke ho. Din shuru ho gaya, aur wo doosron ke reaction se shuru hua.

Doosre mein, bees minute aapke hain — kisi aur cheez ko andar aane se pehle.

Yeh subah nek banne ki baat nahi hai. Yeh is baat ki hai ki sur kaun tay karta hai. Jo pehle andar aata hai uska baaki sab par asar na-barabar hota hai — kuch isliye ki us window mein dimaag asaadharan roop se chhap le leta hai, aur kuch isliye ki jo mood pehle ban gaya, uske through hi har baad ki ghatna padhi jaati hai.

Ek kaam laayak bees minute aisa dikhta hai, aur ismein kuch bhi dramatic nahi hai.

Pehle paani aur roshni. Khidki kholo ya bahar niklo. Yeh dono simple physical signal hain ki din shuru ho gaya, aur yeh pehli coffee se zyada sajgta dete hain.

Phir dus minute ki khamoshi, jis roop mein aap karte ho. Chup baithna, ek vichaar jaan bujh kar pakadna, ya chhota meditation. Dus zyada ho to teen karo. Rozana kiye gaye teen minute kabhi kabhi kiye gaye bees minute se behtar hain.

Phir din ke baare mein ek line. Kaam ki list nahi — ek iraada. Aaj main maa ke saath sabr rakhna chahta hoon. Aaj main wo kaam khatam karunga jise taal raha hoon. Ek sentence, aur aapko hairani hogi ki wo theek us waqt kitni baar yaad aata hai jab uski zaroorat hoti hai.

Aur uske baad hi phone.

Kuch practical bachav. Phone bedroom ke bahar charge karo, kyunki subah chhe baje willpower koi asli cheez nahi hai. Jo chahiye — journal, mat, kursi — raat ko hi nikaal kar rakh do, taaki subah mein koi faisla bache hi nahi. Aur agar ghar bhara hua hai, to jo sabse pehla slot mile wahi lo, chahe wo baaki logon ke uthne se sirf dus minute pehle ho.

Ek imaandaar chhoot. Kuch subhein tooti hui hongi — bimaar bachcha, jaldi ki meeting, bina neend wali raat. Un dinon sabse chhota version lo: khidki par ek minute, ek soch samajh kar li gayi saans, dimaag mein ek line. Sunne mein itna chhota lagta hai ki kya farq padega. Padta hai, kyunki aap bees minute nahi bacha rahe. Aap wo aadat bacha rahe ho ki din ki shuruaat aap apne aap se karte ho, doosron ko jawab dene wale ke roop mein nahi.

articles.title: Do One Hard Thing a Day, Early
articles.titleHinglish: Din Mein Ek Mushkil Kaam, Subah Hi
articles.content:
Everyone has a list of things they are avoiding. The call to the bank. The message that needs an honest answer. The document nobody wants to start. Individually, none of these takes long. Together, they produce a constant background weight that most people mistake for tiredness.

The cost of avoidance is almost never the task. It is the carrying. A ten-minute phone call postponed for eleven days costs ten minutes plus eleven days of low-level dread, which is a terrible exchange rate and one almost everybody accepts daily.

So the practice is simple: one avoided thing, early, before the day fills up.

Why early? Because avoidance grows with the day. At 9am a difficult task is a task; by 7pm it has become a symbol of everything you did not manage. Also, the day will always find something to fill itself with, and the thing you are avoiding will be the item that gets displaced.

A few things that make it work.

Write the list down first. Most people avoid a vague cloud of tasks rather than a specific set, and the cloud is heavier than its contents. When written out, the majority of items take under fifteen minutes each, which is often a shock.

Make the first action absurdly small. Not resolve the dispute, but: open the email and write the first line. Avoidance attaches to the whole task; it rarely survives the first thirty seconds of contact.

Do not negotiate at the moment. Decide the night before which thing it will be, so that in the morning you are executing a decision rather than making one while reluctant.

And notice the relief afterwards, deliberately. This sounds soft and it is mechanically useful — the mind needs evidence that the feared task was smaller than the dread. That evidence is what makes the next one easier.

One caution about the version that goes too far. This is not a call to fill your day with unpleasantness or to treat discomfort as inherently virtuous. It is one thing, once, early. The purpose is not toughness. It is to stop paying rent on tasks you could have finished before breakfast.

And on the days you cannot face it at all — genuinely low days, not merely reluctant ones — pick the smallest item on the list instead, and let that count. The practice is not about proving anything. It is about not letting the pile become the thing that decides how your week feels.
articles.contentHinglish:
Har kisi ke paas un cheezon ki list hoti hai jinse wo bhaag raha hai. Bank ka call. Wo message jiska imaandaar jawab dena hai. Wo document jise koi shuru nahi karna chahta. Alag alag dekho to inme se kisi mein zyada waqt nahi lagta. Milkar yeh ek lagataar background ka bojh banate hain jise zyadatar log thakan samajh lete hain.

Taalne ki keemat lagbhag kabhi kaam nahi hoti. Keemat uthaye rakhna hoti hai. Dus minute ka phone call gyarah din taalne par kharcha hota hai dus minute plus gyarah din ka halka dar — jo bahut hi bura exchange rate hai aur jise lagbhag har koi roz sweekar karta hai.

Toh practice simple hai: ek taali hui cheez, subah, isse pehle ki din bhar jaaye.

Subah kyun? Kyunki taal-matol din ke saath badhti hai. Subah nau baje ek mushkil kaam sirf kaam hai; shaam saat baje tak wo us sab ka pratik ban chuka hota hai jo aapse nahi hua. Aur din khud ko bharne ke liye kuch na kuch dhoondh hi lega, aur jise aap taal rahe ho wahi cheez baahar hogi.

Kuch cheezein jo isse chalati hain.

Pehle list likh lo. Zyadatar log kisi specific set se nahi, kaamon ke ek dhundhle baadal se bhaag rahe hote hain, aur baadal apne saamaan se bhaari hota hai. Likhne par zyadatar cheezein pandrah minute se kam ki nikalti hain, jo aksar chaunka deta hai.

Pehla kadam haasyaspad had tak chhota rakho. "Jhagda suljhao" nahi, balki: email kholo aur pehli line likho. Taal-matol poore kaam se chipakti hai; wo pehle tees second ke sampark ke baad shayad hi zinda rehti hai.

Us waqt mol-bhav mat karo. Raat ko hi tay kar lo ki kaunsi cheez hogi, taaki subah aap faisla le nahi rahe ho, sirf lagu kar rahe ho.

Aur baad wali raahat ko jaan bujh kar notice karo. Sunne mein narm lagta hai aur yeh mechanically kaam ka hai — dimaag ko saboot chahiye ki dara hua kaam us dar se chhota tha. Wahi saboot agli baar aasaan banata hai.

Us version ke liye ek chetavani jo zyada aage chala jaata hai. Yeh apne din ko takleef se bharne ki baat nahi hai, na hi yeh ki asuvidha khud mein koi nekii hai. Ek cheez, ek baar, subah. Maqsad kathorta nahi hai. Maqsad un kaamon ka kiraya dena band karna hai jo nashte se pehle khatam ho sakte the.

Aur jin dinon bilkul himmat na ho — sach mein bhaari din, sirf mann na hone wale nahi — to list ki sabse chhoti cheez uthao aur usi ko gino. Yeh practice kuch sabit karne ke liye nahi hai. Yeh isliye hai ki wo dher aapke poore hafte ka mood tay na kare.
